newsitem.title: UK: UK group sees drawbacks in EMU debt redenomination.
newsitem.headline: UK group sees drawbacks in EMU debt redenomination.

text.p: A working group set up by the Bank of England (BOE) to look at technical issues of a single European currency said on Wednesday it saw more disadvantages in redenominating non-government debt than advantages.
"There are likely to be substantial costs involved," said John Townend, deputy director of the BOE, speaking at an EMU conference in London.

"In particular under English law, it seems likely that bondholder meetings will be required to approve redenomination.... The market group's view is that contractual rights of bondholders should not be removed by legislation."
Townend said the conclusions of the working group were due to be published next week.
He added that if issuers decided to redenominate they should use a limited number of methods agreed by market groups.
The working group also looked at whether market conventions covering technical aspects of debt issuance and trading should be harmonised across the European Union, Townend said.

"The market group is broadly in favour of harmonising market conventions on best international practice and they believe that EMU presents an opportunity to move towards harmonisation, even though there are costs involved and tax differentials will remain."
He said the group recommended harmonisation should apply to new issues after a given date, such as January 1, 1999, when the euro single currency is due to be introduced.
But where it involved changes to issue terms, existing issues should be allowed to run off, he said.

The market group also recommended that euro money markets should follow the European Monetary Institute (EMI) recommendations of an interest day count based on 360 days, rather than 365 as is used in Britain.

He said the group also recommended that business days should be based on daus when clearing systems Cedel and Euroclear and the planned Target system were open. Euro-Libor should be based on London trading days only, the group believed.
